claim: CD47 is ubiquitously expressed and acts as a ligand of signaling regulatory protein (SIRP)α, a critical inhibitory receptor on macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs).
source: CD47 is ubiquitously expressed and acts as a ligand of signaling regulatory protein (SIRP)α, a critical inhibitory receptor on macrophages and dendritic cells (DCs).
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about CD47 and SIRPα.

claim: CD47KO cells are vigorously rejected by macrophages after infusion into syngeneic wild-type (WT) mice.
source: CD47KO cells are vigorously rejected by macrophages after infusion into syngeneic wild-type (WT) mice, demonstrating that CD47 provides a 'don't eat me' signal to macrophages (Oldenborg et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47 provides a 'don't eat me' signal to macrophages.
source: CD47KO cells are vigorously rejected by macrophages after infusion into syngeneic wild-type (WT) mice, demonstrating that CD47 provides a 'don't eat me' signal to macrophages (Oldenborg et al., 2000; Wang et al., 2007a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The strong rejection of xenogeneic cells by macrophages is largely caused by the lack of functional interaction between donor CD47 and recipient SIRPα.
source: We reported that the strong rejection of xenogeneic cells by macrophages (Abe et al., 2002) is largely caused by the lack of functional interaction between donor CD47 and recipient SIRPα (Wang et al., 2007b, Ide et al., 2007; Navarro-Alvarez and Yang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Human CD47 transgenic pigs have achieved encouraging results in pig-to-nonhuman primate xenotransplantation.
source: These findings led to the development of human CD47 transgenic pigs that have achieved encouraging results in pig-to-nonhuman primate xenotransplantation (Tena et al., 2017; Nomura et al., 2020; Watanabe et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47-SIRPα signaling inhibits DC activation and their ability to prime T cells.
source: Importantly, CD47-SIRPα signaling also inhibits DC activation and their ability to prime T cells, and plays an important role in induction of T cell tolerance by donor-specific transfusion (DST) and hepatocyte transplantation (Wang et al., 2007a, Wang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47-SIRPα signaling plays an important role in induction of T cell tolerance by donor-specific transfusion (DST) and hepatocyte transplantation.
source: Importantly, CD47-SIRPα signaling also inhibits DC activation and their ability to prime T cells, and plays an important role in induction of T cell tolerance by donor-specific transfusion (DST) and hepatocyte transplantation (Wang et al., 2007a, Wang et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Transgenic expression of human CD47 in pigs may attenuate xenoimmune responses by ameliorating DC activation and antigen presentation.
source: Thus, transgenic expression of human CD47 in pigs may also attenuate xenoimmune responses by ameliorating DC activation and antigen presentation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the previous findings about CD47-SIRPα signaling effects on DC activation.

claim: Transgenic overexpression of CD47 was applied for reducing allogenicity and generating hypoimmunogenic pluripotent stem cells.
source: More recently, transgenic overexpression of CD47 was also applied for reducing allogenicity and generating hypoimmunogenic pluripotent stem cells (Han et al., 2019; Deuse et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47 upregulation was detected in various cancer cells, serving a powerful mechanism of evading macrophage killing.
source: CD47 upregulation was detected in various cancer cells, serving a powerful mechanism of evading macrophage killing (Jaiswal et al., 2009; Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Treatment with CD47 blockade could inhibit tumor growth via macrophage-mediated mechanism.
source: Accordingly, treatment with CD47 blockade could inhibit tumor growth via macrophage-mediated mechanism (Jaiswal et al., 2009; Willingham et al., 2012; Weiskopf et al., 2016; Chao et al., 2010; Liu et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: The antitumor activity of CD47 blockade was found to be associated with CD11c+ DC activation and largely T cell-dependent.
source: More recently, the antitumor activity of CD47 blockade was found to be associated with CD11c+ DC activation and largely T cell-dependent (Liu et al., 2015b, Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes (Exos) from cells transgenically overexpressing CD47 or tumor cells overexpressing endogenous CD47, could induce CD47 cross-dressing on pig or human cells.
source: We found that extracellular vesicles (EVs), including exosomes (Exos) from cells transgenically overexpressing CD47 or tumor cells overexpressing endogenous CD47, could induce CD47 cross-dressing on pig or human cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD47 cross-dressed on cell surfaces can interact with SIRPα to inhibit phagocytosis.
source: CD47 cross-dressed on cell surfaces can interact with SIRPα to inhibit phagocytosis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Ligation of the autogenous, but not cross-dressed, CD47 induced cell death.
source: However, ligation of the autogenous, but not cross-dressed, CD47 induced cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing provides an alternative source of cell surface CD47 that may elicit its anti-phagocytic function without transmitting harmful signals to the cells.
source: Thus, CD47 cross-dressing provides an alternative source of cell surface CD47 that may elicit its anti-phagocytic function without transmitting harmful signals to the cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings about cross-dressed CD47 function.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing suggests a previously unidentified mechanism for tumor-induced immunosuppression.
source: CD47 cross-dressing also suggests a previously unidentified mechanism for tumor-induced immunosuppression.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: PAOC/CD47p cells showed significantly increased CD47 staining after coculture with PAOC/CD47p/h2 or PAOC/CD47p/h4.
source: Flow cytometry analysis using anti-CD47 antibodies recognizing both human and pig CD47 revealed that PAOC/CD47p/h2 or PAOC/CD47p/h4 cells expressed a markedly increased level of CD47 compared to PAOC/CD47p cells, and that PAOC/CD47p cells showed significantly increased CD47 staining after coculture with PAOC/CD47p/h2 or PAOC/CD47p/h4 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PAOC/CD47p cells were cross-dressed by CD47, likely transgenic hCD47, from PAOC/CD47p/h cells during cultures.
source: These results suggest that PAOC/CD47p cells were cross-dressed by CD47, likely transgenic hCD47, from PAOC/CD47p/h cells during cultures.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: PAOC47null cells became positively stained by both anti-h/pCD47 and anti-hCD47 antibodies after coculture with PAOC/CD47h2 or PAOC/CD47h4 cells.
source: When the PAOC cell line cells were cocultured for 24 hr, we found that PAOC47null cells became positively stained by both anti-h/pCD47 (Figure 1B, top) and anti-hCD47 (Figure 1B, bottom) antibodies.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PAOC/CD47null cells can be cross-dressed by CD47 after coculture with PAOC/CD47h2 cells.
source: This experiment, in which fluorescence-labeling allowed for better distinguishing between the two cell populations in the cocultures, further confirmed that PAOC/CD47null cells can be cross-dressed by CD47 after coculture with PAOC/CD47h2 cells (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: PAOC cells express SIRPα.
source: PAOC cells express SIRPα (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, left), and pig SIRPα is reported to interact with human CD47 (Boettcher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous research.

claim: Pig SIRPα is reported to interact with human CD47.
source: PAOC cells express SIRPα (Figure 1—figure supplement 2, left), and pig SIRPα is reported to interact with human CD47 (Boettcher et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The interaction of CD47 with SIRPα may facilitate lentiviral engulfment by target cells.
source: Furthermore, previous studies have shown that CD47-lentiviruses are more effective in transducing SIRPα+ non-phagocytic tumor cells, suggesting that the interaction of CD47 with SIRPα may facilitate lentiviral engulfment by target cells (Sosale et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: LCL cells cocultured with LCL cells that express hCD47 (LCL/CD47p/h), but not those cultured alone or mixed with LCL/CD47p/h immediately prior to flow cytometry analysis, were positively stained by anti-hCD47 antibodies.
source: LCL cells cocultured with LCL cells that express hCD47 (LCL/CD47p/h) (Ide et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011), but not those cultured alone or mixed with LCL/CD47p/h immediately prior to flow cytometry analysis, were positively stained by anti-hCD47 antibodies (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing can occur in an SIRPα-independent manner.
source: Although we cannot rule out of the role of SIRPα in hCD47 cross-dressing, our data indicate that hCD47 cross-dressing can occur in an SIRPα-independent manner.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: PAOC47null cells became positively stained by anti-hCD47 antibodies after being cocultured with hCD47-tg swine cells.
source: Like pig cells cocultured with hCD47-transgenic cell lines (Figure 1A–D), PAOC47null cells also became positively stained by anti-hCD47 antibodies after being cocultured with hCD47-tg swine cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Jurkat cells express a higher level of CD47 than normal hematopoietic cells.
source: We next determined whether cells can be cross-dressed by native CD47 using human T-cell leukemia Jurkat cells that express a higher level of CD47 than normal hematopoietic cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD47KO Jurkat cells were clearly stained positive by anti-hCD47 antibodies after coculture with parental WT Jurkat cells or hCD47-tg pig LCL cells compared to those cultured alone or mixed immediately before staining.
source: Flow cytometry analysis revealed that CD47KO Jurkat cells were clearly stained positive by anti-hCD47 antibodies after coculture with parental WT Jurkat cells or hCD47-tg pig LCL cells compared to those cultured alone or mixed immediately before staining (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pig LCL cells became positive for human CD47 staining after coculture for 24 hr with WT Jurkat cells.
source: Furthermore, pig LCL cells also became positive for human CD47 staining after coculture for 24 hr with WT Jurkat cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: More than half of the cross-dressed hCD47 remained on pig LCL cells 3 days after being separated from hCD47-expressing cells.
source: More than half of the cross-dressed hCD47 (determined by MFI) remained on pig LCL cells 3 days after being separated from hCD47-expressing cells (Figure 2C), indicating that hCD47 cross-dressing was relatively stable.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing was relatively stable.
source: More than half of the cross-dressed hCD47 (determined by MFI) remained on pig LCL cells 3 days after being separated from hCD47-expressing cells (Figure 2C), indicating that hCD47 cross-dressing was relatively stable.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Not only hCD47, but other membrane proteins of WT Jurkat cells were also cross-dressed on pig LCL cells.
source: We also noted that not only hCD47, but other membrane proteins of WT Jurkat cells were also cross-dressed on pig LCL cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing was clearly detected on LCL cells that were pretreated with cytochalasin D after cocultured with cytochalasin D-pretreated WT Jurkat cells, though the level was lower than untreated cells.
source: While to a lower level than untreated cells, hCD47 cross-dressing was clearly detected on LCL cells that were pretreated with cytochalasin D, a cell-permeable potent inhibitor that disrupts actin microfilaments (Cooper, 1987), after cocultured with cytochalasin D-pretreated WT Jurkat cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that a functional cytoskeleton is not absolutely required for, but may facilitate hCD47 cross-dressing.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: A functional cytoskeleton is not absolutely required for, but may facilitate hCD47 cross-dressing.
source: While to a lower level than untreated cells, hCD47 cross-dressing was clearly detected on LCL cells that were pretreated with cytochalasin D, a cell-permeable potent inhibitor that disrupts actin microfilaments (Cooper, 1987), after cocultured with cytochalasin D-pretreated WT Jurkat cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), indicating that a functional cytoskeleton is not absolutely required for, but may facilitate hCD47 cross-dressing.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Human CD47 cross-dressing could be induced by not only hCD47-transgenic cells but also tumor cells that express only the native CD47.
source: These results indicate that human CD47 cross-dressing could be induced by not only hCD47-transgenic cells but also tumor cells that express only the native CD47.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing occurred in both CD47KO human T-cell leukemia Jurkat cells and pig B-lymphoma LCL cells after incubation for 2 or 6 hr with PAOC47h2 cell-derived EVs.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that CD47 cross-dressing occurred in both CD47KO human T-cell leukemia Jurkat cells (Figure 3A) and pig B-lymphoma LCL cells (Figure 3B) after incubation for 2 or 6 hr with PAOC47h2 cell-derived EVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Both CD47KO Jurkat and LCL cells were positively stained by anti-hCD47 after incubation with Exos released by PAOC47h2 cells, though to a less extent than EVs.
source: To a less extent, both CD47KO Jurkat and LCL cells were also positively stained by anti-hCD47 after incubation with Exos released by PAOC47h2 cells (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing was detected in PAOCnull cells after incubation with EVs from PAOC47h2 cells.
source: Similarly, hCD47 cross-dressing was detected in PAOCnull cells after incubation with EVs from PAOC47h2 cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A significant proportion of violet-labeled PAOCnull cells became positive for hCD47 after incubation with PAOC47h2 EVs.
source: After incubation with PAOC47h2 EVs, a significant proportion of violet-labeled PAOCnull cells became positive for hCD47 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The frequency of hCD47+ PAOCnull cells at 42 hr was lower than that at 18 hr, which is most likely due to PAOCnull cell proliferation and EV exhaustion/degradation.
source: Of note, the frequency of hCD47+ PAOCnull cells at 42 hr was lower than that at 18 hr, which is most likely due to PAOCnull cell proliferation and EV exhaustion/degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Pig LCL cells were stained positive for hCD47 after incubated with EVs from hCD47-tg pig LCL cells or WT Jurkat cells.
source: Pig LCL cells were also stained positive for hCD47 after incubated with EVs from hCD47-tg pig LCL cells or WT Jurkat cells, in which hCD47 cross-dressing was detected 1 hr after incubation with EVs and the levels remained stable or increased at 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing was detected 1 hr after incubation with EVs and the levels remained stable or increased at 24 hr.
source: Pig LCL cells were also stained positive for hCD47 after incubated with EVs from hCD47-tg pig LCL cells or WT Jurkat cells, in which hCD47 cross-dressing was detected 1 hr after incubation with EVs and the levels remained stable or increased at 24 hr (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing could be induced independently of cell-cell contact by EVs, including Exos.
source: These results indicate that CD47 cross-dressing could be induced independently of cell-cell contact by EVs, including Exos.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: hCD47 was clearly detected on cytochalasin D-pretreated LCL cells after incubation with EVs from hCD47-tg LCL cells, though the level was moderately reduced.
source: Again, a functional cytoskeleton is not absolutely required for hCD47 cross-dressing, as hCD47 was clearly detected on cytochalasin D-pretreated LCL cells after incubation with EVs from hCD47-tg LCL cells, though the level was moderately reduced (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Cross-dressing was not diminished by treatment with trypsin/EDTA, indicating that membrane fusion is involved in EV cross-dressing.
source: Furthermore, cross-dressing was not diminished by treatment with trypsin/EDTA, indicating that membrane fusion is involved in EV cross-dressing (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and inference from the data.

claim: Human SIRPα fusion protein was able to bind CD47KO Jurkat cells cultured with EVs but not those cultured without EVs.
source: Flow cytometry analysis showed that human SIRPα fusion protein was able to bind CD47KO Jurkat cells cultured with EVs but not those cultured without EVs (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Cross-dressed hCD47 on CD47KO Jurkat cells can bind human SIRPα.
source: The data indicate that cross-dressed hCD47 on CD47KO Jurkat cells can bind human SIRPα.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: PAOC47null cells were significantly more sensitive than PAOC/CD47h2 cells to phagocytosis.
source: As expected, PAOC47null cells were significantly more sensitive than PAOC/CD47h2 cells to phagocytosis (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressing effectively reduced the susceptibility of PAOC47null cells to phagocytosis by human macrophages, to a level comparable to that of PAOC/CD47h2 cells.
source: However, hCD47 cross-dressing effectively reduced the susceptibility of PAOC47null cells to phagocytosis by human macrophages, to a level comparable to that of PAOC/CD47h2 cells (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Human CD47 cross-dressing protects not only xenogeneic pig cells, but also human leukemia cells, against phagocytosis by human macrophages.
source: Human CD47 cross-dressing protects not only xenogeneic pig cells, but also human leukemia cells, against phagocytosis by human macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: CD47KO Jurkat cells showed significantly greater phagocytosis than WT Jurkat cells.
source: In phagocytic assays where CD47KO Jurkat cells showed significantly greater phagocytosis than WT Jurkat cells, pre-incubation of CD47KO Jurkat cells with EVs released by PAOC/CD47h2 cells was found highly effective in reducing their phagocytosis by human macrophages (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Pre-incubation of CD47KO Jurkat cells with EVs released by PAOC/CD47h2 cells was highly effective in reducing their phagocytosis by human macrophages.
source: In phagocytic assays where CD47KO Jurkat cells showed significantly greater phagocytosis than WT Jurkat cells, pre-incubation of CD47KO Jurkat cells with EVs released by PAOC/CD47h2 cells was found highly effective in reducing their phagocytosis by human macrophages (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Human CD47 cross-dressing can act as a functional ligand for human SIRPα and deliver 'don't eat me' signals to human macrophages.
source: These results indicate that human CD47 cross-dressing can act as a functional ligand for human SIRPα and deliver 'don't eat me' signals to human macrophages.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by its ligand thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
source: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by its ligand thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) (Saumet et al., 2005), CD47-binding peptides of TSP-1 (Martinez-Torres et al., 2015) or CD47 antibodies (Mateo et al., 1999) has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by CD47-binding peptides of TSP-1 has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
source: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by its ligand thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) (Saumet et al., 2005), CD47-binding peptides of TSP-1 (Martinez-Torres et al., 2015) or CD47 antibodies (Mateo et al., 1999) has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by CD47 antibodies has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
source: Ligation of cell surface CD47 by its ligand thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) (Saumet et al., 2005), CD47-binding peptides of TSP-1 (Martinez-Torres et al., 2015) or CD47 antibodies (Mateo et al., 1999) has been shown to induce death in varying types of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Human SIRPα-Fc fusion proteins could induce cell death in a dose-dependent manner in WT, but not CD47KO, human T-cell leukemia Jurkat cells.
source: In line with these reports, we observed that human SIRPα-Fc fusion proteins could induce cell death in a dose-dependent manner in WT, but not CD47KO, human T-cell leukemia Jurkat cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figures 5A and B.

claim: The cell death observed in WT Jurkat cells was induced by CD47 ligation with hSIRPα-Fc proteins.
source: The cell death observed in WT Jurkat cells was induced by CD47 ligation with hSIRPα-Fc proteins, as cell death was minimally detectable in WT Jurkat cells that were cultured simultaneously without hSIRPα-Fc proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: SIRPα-Fc proteins induced significant cell death in WT Jurkat cells regardless of whether they were cocultured with CD47KO or with hCD47 cross-dressed CD47KO.
source: We found that SIRPα-Fc proteins induced significant cell death in WT Jurkat cells regardless of whether they were cocultured with CD47KO (Figure 5C and D) or with hCD47 cross-dressed CD47KO (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C, D, E, and F.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing did not increase the sensitivity to cell death induced by SIRPα-Fc proteins.
source: CD47 cross-dressing did not increase the sensitivity to cell death induced by SIRPα-Fc proteins, and cell death was minimally detectable in both CD47KO (Figure 5C and D) and hCD47 cross-dressed CD47KO (Figure 5E and F) Jurkat cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C, D, E, and F.

claim: Cell death was minimally detectable in both CD47KO and hCD47 cross-dressed CD47KO Jurkat cells.
source: CD47 cross-dressing did not increase the sensitivity to cell death induced by SIRPα-Fc proteins, and cell death was minimally detectable in both CD47KO (Figure 5C and D) and hCD47 cross-dressed CD47KO (Figure 5E and F) Jurkat cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C, D, E, and F.

claim: CD47KO Jurkat cells regained the sensitivity to apoptosis induced by CD47 agonists after being transfected to express CD47.
source: However, CD47KO Jurkat cells regained the sensitivity to apoptosis induced by CD47 agonists after being transfected to express CD47 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Unlike autogenous CD47, cross-dressed CD47 on Jurkat cells does not induce cell death upon ligation with SIRPα-Fc proteins.
source: These results indicate that, unlike autogenous CD47, cross-dressed CD47 on Jurkat cells does not induce cell death upon ligation with SIRPα-Fc proteins.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental data.

claim: EVs and Exos released from pig cells transgenically overexpressing hCD47 can mediate hCD47 cross-dressing on surrounding pig cells.
source: Here we found that EVs and Exos released from pig cells transgenically overexpressing hCD47 can mediate hCD47 cross-dressing on surrounding pig cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: hCD47 cross-dressed on pig cells can interact with human SIRPα and inhibit phagocytosis by human macrophages.
source: Furthermore, hCD47 cross-dressed on pig cells can interact with human SIRPα and inhibit phagocytosis by human macrophages.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing occurs not only in the pig-to-pig combination, but also in the human-to-human, pig-to-human, and human-to-pig directions.
source: Such CD47 cross-dressing occurs not only in the pig-to-pig combination, but also in the human-to-human, pig-to-human, and human-to-pig directions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A high level of transgenic CD47 expression was found to be essential for its immune inhibitory effect in both xenogeneic and allogeneic settings.
source: In both xenogeneic and allogeneic settings, a high level of transgenic CD47 expression was found to be essential for its immune inhibitory effect.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: CD47 is not only a ligand of SIRPα, but also a signaling receptor that mediates a variety of functions, including apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, and senescence.
source: CD47 is not only a ligand of SIRPα, but also a signaling receptor that mediates a variety of functions, including apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, and senescence.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Deletion of CD47 improves survival, proliferation, and function of endothelial cells, leading to increased angiogenesis and neovascularization both in vitro and in vivo.
source: It was reported that deletion of CD47 improves survival, proliferation, and function of endothelial cells, leading to increased angiogenesis and neovascularization both in vitro and in vivo (Meijles et al., 2017; Gao et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47 deletion from organ grafts was reported to ameliorate renal ischemia/reperfusion injury.
source: In line with these observations, CD47 deletion from organ grafts was reported to ameliorate renal ischemia/reperfusion injury (Isenberg and Roberts, 2019) and cardiac allograft rejection (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47 deletion from organ grafts was reported to ameliorate cardiac allograft rejection.
source: In line with these observations, CD47 deletion from organ grafts was reported to ameliorate renal ischemia/reperfusion injury (Isenberg and Roberts, 2019) and cardiac allograft rejection (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: Widespread expression of hCD47 in the pig kidney was associated with increased vascular permeability and systemic edema, presumably due to upregulated TSP-1, and hence, TSP-1-CD47 signaling in the graft.
source: Using a pig-to-baboon kidney xenotransplantation model, a recent study suggested that widespread expression of hCD47 in the pig kidney was associated with increased vascular permeability and systemic edema, presumably due to upregulated TSP-1, and hence, TSP-1-CD47 signaling in the graft (Takeuchi et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Ligation of hSIRPα-Fc proteins with autogenous, but not cross-dressed, CD47 on Jurkat cells induces cell death.
source: We found that ligation of hSIRPα-Fc proteins with autogenous, but not cross-dressed, CD47 on Jurkat cells induces cell death.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Using a pig vascularized organ with hCD47 overexpression in some cells, which are more sensitive to macrophage attack but relatively resistant to CD47 signaling-induced deleterious effects, may improve the outcomes of xenotransplantation.
source: This study suggests that using a pig vascularized organ with hCD47 overexpression in some cells, which are more sensitive to macrophage attack but relatively resistant to CD47 signaling-induced deleterious effects, may improve the outcomes of xenotransplantation.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: CD47 cross-dressed on cells, which induces sufficient SIRPα signaling to inhibit macrophages, may suppress SIRPα+ DC activation.
source: Although it was not tested directly, it is conceivable that CD47 cross-dressed on cells, which induces sufficient SIRPα signaling to inhibit macrophages, may suppress SIRPα+ DC activation.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: In addition to inhibition of phagocytosis, CD47 cross-dressing may also attenuate anti-donor T cell responses when transplants are performed using CD47-overexpressing donors.
source: Thus, in addition to inhibition of phagocytosis, CD47 cross-dressing may also attenuate anti-donor T cell responses when transplants are performed using CD47-overexpressing donors.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings.

claim: CD47 upregulation in tumors significantly contributes to tumor-induced T cell suppression.
source: CD47 upregulation in tumors also significantly contributes to tumor-induced T cell suppression, as the antitumor activity of CD47 blocking treatment is associated with CD11c+ DC activation and is largely T cell-dependent (Liu et al., 2015b, Chen et al., 2020; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing was found in human T-cell leukemia Jurkat and pig B-lymphoma LCL cells.
source: In the present study, CD47 cross-dressing was found in human T-cell leukemia Jurkat and pig B-lymphoma LCL cells, suggesting a possible involvement of CD47 cross-dressing in the formation of a tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: CD47 cross-dressing may be involved in the formation of a tumor immunosuppressive microenvironment.

claim: CD47 on EVs and CD47 cross-dressed on tumor cells may neutralize CD47 ligands, such as TSP-1 that has been shown to induce CD47 activation leading to apoptosis in tumor and endothelial cells, hence, favoring tumor growth.
source: In addition, CD47 on EVs and CD47 cross-dressed on tumor cells may also neutralize CD47 ligands, such as TSP-1 that has been shown to induce CD47 activation leading to apoptosis in tumor and endothelial cells (Martinez-Torres et al., 2015), hence, favoring tumor growth.
evidence: This claim is based on speculation about the implications of the findings and citation to previous research.

claim: CD47, as a 'don't eat me' signal, is essential for EVs to elicit biological function by preventing their clearance by macrophages.
source: Earlier studies have shown that CD47, as a 'don't eat me' signal, is essential for EVs to elicit biological function by preventing their clearance by macrophages (Kamerkar et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: EV-induced CD47 cross-dressing possesses partial activity of the autogenous CD47, such as the ability to initiate inhibitory SIRPα signaling.
source: Here we report that EV-induced CD47 cross-dressing possesses partial activity of the autogenous CD47, such as the ability to initiate inhibitory SIRPα signaling, and therefore offers means of separating the desired and harmful effects of CD47.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.
